method.instrument: Automated Winkler titrator, UV end-point detector

why.text: Below the mixed layer off Southern California oxygen has fallen since the 1980s and the hypoxic boundary has risen toward the shelf, squeezing the habitat of fish and invertebrates.
Oxygen is the balance of what the ocean takes in at the surface and what animals and bacteria use below; a warmer ocean holds less and mixes less, so it is losing oxygen.
Warming thins the oxygen the surface layer can hold, and the upper ocean has been losing it for decades across the North Pacific, not only here.
How large are the ocean’s “dead zones” and how fast are they changing?
Is the biomass of the ocean changing?

steps: incubated at the simulated light level

why.text: Chlorophyll says how much plant life is there; the ¹⁴C incubation says how fast it is growing, and primary production is the term that connects the ocean’s plankton to the climate and to the fish.
A dark bottle is incubated beside the lit ones so that whatever is taken up without light can be subtracted from the rest.
Is the biomass of the ocean changing?

why.text: Light is the other half of photosynthesis: how deep it reaches sets the bottom of the layer where anything can grow, and the water’s own plankton is what dims it.
Surface light and light at depth are measured together so a cast can be read as a fraction of that day’s sun rather than an absolute.

why.text: The North Pacific High is what sets the coastal wind, and how strong and how far north it sits in winter shapes the upwelling and the productivity of the season that follows.
Pressure at the ship is one point in that pattern; it is read against the basin-scale fields, not alone.

why.text: Only wind along the coast drives upwelling, and only in one direction, so the direction decides whether a given wind speed feeds the system or shuts it down.
A wind direction recorded relative to a moving ship is not the same as a wind direction over the ground.

why.text: Winds blowing toward the equator along the coast push surface water offshore and pull cold, nutrient-rich water up from below: the engine of the California Current’s productivity.
Wind also mixes the surface layer: a windy spell deepens the mixed layer and brings nutrients up even far from the coast.

why.text: Evaporation is the largest way the ocean loses heat, and how dry the air above it is drives that loss month by month across the North Pacific.
Humidity is needed with wind and air temperature to compute the heat the surface is losing at all.
